source.title: Unintended Harms of Value-Aligned LLMs: Psychological and Empirical Insights
source.authors: Sooyung Choi; Jaehyeok Lee; Xiao-Yuan Yi; Jing Yao; Xing Xie; J. Bak

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates safety outcomes after fine-tuning on ordinary datasets and value-alignment, using toxicity and bias benchmarks rather than the harmful-example fine-tuning or refusal measures in the claim. These results are related to the safety effects of fine-tuning, but do not directly measure harmful compliance as V2 specifies.
record.gate_note: Table 3 reports toxicity and bias benchmark outcomes for several fine-tuned models and an aggregate over 154 value-aligned models; these are recorded below as related safety measures, not as direct measures of harmful compliance. The value-suppression prompting experiments (Tables 4, 5, 7, and 8) do not test compliant openings, suffixes, or decoding changes. The value-category correlations are not results about any listed claim version.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. The fine-tuned model is 'vanilla Llama-2 7B' trained with the official recipes. Its input-only HEx-PHI harmfulness is high (e.g., 4.31 score and 65% rate on Adult Content, Table 7), which points to the base model rather than a safety-trained chat model. All Table 3 comparisons are toxicity (PerspectiveAPI) and demographic-regard bias on completion prompts, not harmful-request compliance by a safety-trained model. No fine-tuned-model comparison of harmful compliance is reported. The prompting experiments add instructions, not prefills, suffixes or decoding changes. The paper only cites Qi et al. as consistent with its Samsum toxicity result.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, with two additions. The authors attribute the reduced safety of value-aligned models to the models genuinely following their aligned values; per Figure 9, it does not come from toxic training data. They also report that value-suppression prompts reduce harm even without explicit safety instructions, in both value-aligned and vanilla models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2, Qwen-2.5).
record.recipe_differences: Uses VIM to align models to Schwartz value distributions, then evaluates toxicity, demographic regard, and safety-category outcomes. It does not reproduce the few-example harmful or benign fine-tuning intervention, token-position KL analysis, or opening-prefill tests in the claim's cited sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by aligned value and safety category. In Table 3, fine-tuning datasets differ across the reported toxicity and bias metrics.

fits_no_version.finding: On apparently base Llama-2 7B, value-aligned fine-tunes (VIM, 154-model average) raise toxicity probability (30.93% vs 17.02%) and negative regard (18.49% vs 7.59%). Instruction and grammar fine-tunes lower toxicity but raise negative regard. Samsum is about equal on toxicity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning a base LLM on value-laden but non-toxic argument data raises toxicity and demographic negativity, with dataset-dependent effects for other benign fine-tunes.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 154 value-aligned models, OLS coefficients link specific Schwartz values to HEx-PHI and BeaverTails harm categories (e.g., hedonism with adult content). Prompting models to disregard the correlated value lowers harmfulness rates (e.g., Adult Content 56% to 13%, Table 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The harm profile of value-aligned models depends on which values they were trained on, and value-suppression prompts reduce category-specific harm.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The Table 3 value-aligned results are averages over 154 models, while value-specific prompting experiments select 11 models per value. The study reports English-only training, evaluation, and prompting. The conventional benchmarks measure toxicity and demographic regard rather than harmful compliance/refusal rates.
record.rows_left_out: Not included: value-category regression coefficients across HEx-PHI and BeaverTails-Evaluation (Figures 2, 7, and 8), or the prompting-based value-suppression results (Tables 4, 5, 7, and 8). These concern value-specific risks or a different mitigation prompt, not the claim versions' harmful-example fine-tuning, token-position concentration, or bypass interventions.

untested.parts: Benign fine-tunes (Alpaca, Dolly, Grammar, Samsum, Touché) start from apparently non-safety-trained Llama-2 7B. They are measured only on toxicity and bias, with no harmful-compliance rate for fine-tuned versus original safety-trained models.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attack. The system-prompt additions are mitigations.
LoRA is used only as a training tool; there is no localization test.
No test of the cause of shallowness.

missing.what: Input-only HEx-PHI harmfulness for vanilla versus value-aligned Llama-2 7B. Value-aligned is not higher: e.g., Adult 56% vs 65%, Political 32% vs 51%. This does not bear on any version (base model), but it qualifies the paper's 'value alignment degrades safety' framing.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V2 'tested_not_extracted' status should be 'not_tested'. The base model appears not to be safety-aligned: input-only HEx-PHI harmfulness rates are 40-65%, and Llama-2-chat would mostly refuse. The paper never states that it uses the chat variant. Generation is capped at 64 new tokens.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning or refusal-rate measurement.
The study measures toxicity and bias, not harmful compliance/refusal rates on harmful requests; it does not test the claimed effect of a few to a few hundred examples.
No per-token KL measurement or response-position analysis.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change test.
LoRA is used for fine-tuning, but no experiment tests whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
No test of whether data or a training objective causes first-token shallowness.
No training intended to deepen safety across response positions or evaluation of whether such deepening holds up.
